exercise.text_title: The Volunteer Job I Chose for the Wrong Reason
exercise.article:
I first signed up for the community repair workshop with a rather selfish aim: to make my CV look more impressive. I had heard that volunteering could be a great way to gain skills that employers value, and I wanted to have something that stood out on my applications. I imagined myself learning to fix things, which seemed like a useful, practical skill to add to my repertoire.

On my first day, I arrived at the workshop full of enthusiasm, ready to dive into the world of repairs. However, things didn’t go quite as I had planned. Instead of being handed a toolbox, I was asked to greet visitors and find out how we could assist them. It was a role I hadn’t anticipated, and I felt slightly out of my depth. I had expected to be working with my hands, not my voice.

My initial disappointment soon gave way to curiosity. As I welcomed people, I noticed how nervous some were about asking for help. One visitor, in particular, stood out. He came in with a broken lamp and seemed embarrassed about not knowing how to fix it himself. I realised that my job was not just to help with repairs but also to ensure people didn’t feel foolish for needing assistance. I found myself explaining things in a way that was both informative and reassuring.

As the weeks went by, I began to enjoy this unexpected aspect of my role. I learned to coordinate tasks among volunteers, each with different skills, and found that I enjoyed this more than the actual repairing. It was satisfying to see everything come together smoothly, and I took pride in being part of a team that made it happen.

When it came time to update my CV, I paused to reflect on what I had truly gained from the experience. I realised that the most valuable outcome wasn’t the line on my CV, but a new understanding of what I enjoyed in a work environment. I discovered that I was more interested in roles that involved interacting with people and organising tasks than I had previously thought.

This experience taught me that career insights can come from the most unexpected places. I had initially joined the workshop for the wrong reason, but what I learned about myself turned out to be far more important than any skill I could have listed on my CV.
